finding: The live range of $110-$625 is about right for one bolt-in sensor at both ends, though the top is only reached with a dealer-priced sensor and a slow, corroded removal. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2015 Corolla about $93-$659 (0.4-2.0 hr); midsize 2014 Subaru Outback about $90-$403 (0.4-2.0 hr); truck 2016 Silverado 1500 about $98-$396 (0.5-2.0 hr); luxury 2015 BMW 328i about $87-$488 (0.4-2.0 hr). The low ends, about $87-$98, pair an online aftermarket sensor with a manufacturer warranty time and no diagnosis; Subaru pays its dealers a separate 0.5 hr for ABS testing and diagnosis, and Jerry also puts diagnosis at about half an hour, which adds roughly $60-$80, so a real quote rarely comes in under about $150 and $110 is a fair floor. At the top, only the Corolla passes $625, and only because a genuine Toyota front sensor lists at $321-$339 where the others list at $76-$168; with the same two hours the Outback, Silverado and BMW stop at about $400-$490. The benchmarks agree: Jerry gives $189-$357 and up to $600 or more at a shop, and RepairPal's BMW Z4 figure is $295-$346. How solid the labor times are: the low end is solid only for the midsize class, where Subaru states 0.4 hr for one front sensor on the example vehicle. The truck low end is now a pickup maker's own figure, Nissan's 0.5 hr to inspect both front sensors and replace one on a 2019 Titan XD, but that is a comparable full-size pickup, not the Silverado; a Ram 3500 bulletin (0.4 hr, one rear sensor) and a Honda Ridgeline bulletin (0.3 hr, one rear sensor, as an add-on) sit close to it. The economy and luxury classes still borrow the Subaru 0.4 hr, because no stated front-sensor time was found for a Corolla or a BMW; Tesla's service manual (0.30 for a Model 3 or Model Y front sensor, unit not printed) points the same way but is not used. A second pass on 2026-11-20 looked through GM, FCA, Honda and Acura, Hyundai and Kia, Nissan and Infiniti, Mazda and Subaru bulletins for a front-sensor replacement time on a common compact car, half-ton pickup or luxury car and found none: the bulletins that mention wheel speed sensors pay for inspection, cleaning the encoder ring, wiring re-routing, software, or hub replacement instead, and GM's says only to use the published time. The truck example was not switched to the Titan XD because its parts could not be fully re-sourced (the one aftermarket listing found did not state front or rear). Every high end is one general guide's 1 to 2 hours, not a book time; the same guide's customer examples show only 25-35 minutes billed, so most jobs will sit well under the high totals, and the 2 hours is there for sensors seized in a rusted knuckle. Confidence stays low: only one of the eight hours figures is for the example vehicle itself. Where the sensor is part of the hub: on some vehicles the sensor or its encoder ring is built into the hub and bearing assembly, so the hub is replaced instead. Honda's 2006-07 Civic rear sensor recall (bulletin 07-055) replaces the sensor together with the rear hub bearing unit (0.7 hr added for one side), and FCA's recall 24V-794 for the 2025 Ram 1500 fixes a wheel speed fault from the front bearing's encoder ring by replacing the hub and bearing assembly (1.1 hr for one side including road test). Jerry says hub-integrated parts often cost $250-$500 for the part alone. That is the wheel bearing or hub job and is priced there, not here. Rear sensors were not priced. This is an estimate, not a quote and not a diagnosis; an ABS light has other causes, including wiring, the tone ring and the wheel bearing.
extras: A quote often adds an ABS scan and diagnosis fee (about half an hour; Subaru's own bulletin lists 0.5 hr for ABS testing and diagnosis as a separate operation), shop supplies and sales tax. Extra time is common where the old sensor has seized in the knuckle and breaks on removal. Related items quoted separately: wiring or connector repair, cleaning or replacing a rusted tone (reluctor) ring, a wheel bearing or hub assembly where the sensor or encoder ring is part of it, and the sensor on the other side. Some vehicles need a steering angle or stability control calibration after the repair.
